overview:
Jamaica is the third-largest island in the Caribbean, lying south of Cuba and west of Haiti. It covers about 11,000 km², slightly smaller than the US state of Connecticut, and about 2.8 million people call it home. The capital, Kingston, sits on a wide natural harbor on the southeast coast beneath the Blue Mountains.

Few small countries have made such a big mark on the world. Reggae music, born in Kingston's neighborhoods, spread across the globe with Bob Marley, and Jamaican sprinters such as Usain Bolt have dominated Olympic tracks. Jamaican Patois, a lively Creole language, is spoken alongside English, the official language.

Most Jamaicans are descended from Africans brought to the island as slaves, joined by people of Indian, Chinese, European and Middle Eastern heritage, which explains the national motto, "Out of Many, One People." Jamaica is an independent member of the Commonwealth with a parliament and prime minister, and the British monarch as head of state. Tourism, bauxite mining, sugar and Blue Mountain coffee support the economy.
landAndNature:
Mountains fill the interior of Jamaica, climbing to Blue Mountain Peak at about 2,256 meters, where mist swirls around coffee farms that produce some of the world's most prized beans. In the west, Cockpit Country is a maze of steep limestone hills and hidden valleys riddled with caves. Rivers such as the Rio Grande and the Black River wind down to a coast of white beaches in the north and mangrove wetlands in the south.

The climate is tropical, cooler in the mountains, with hurricanes a risk from June to November. The red-billed streamertail hummingbird, called the doctor bird, is the national bird and found only on Jamaica. The island also has the Jamaican boa, crocodiles in the Black River, the giant swallowtail, one of the largest butterflies in the Americas, and colorful reef fish along the coast.
peopleAndCulture:
Jamaican Patois mixes English with West African words and rhythms, and sayings like "wah gwaan" (what's going on) are heard everywhere. Music is the heartbeat: ska, rocksteady, reggae and dancehall all began here, and Rastafari, a faith that grew up in Jamaica in the 1930s, gave reggae its dreadlocks and its message. Sound systems still shake neighborhood streets on weekend nights.

Jerk chicken and pork, rubbed with fiery spices and smoked over pimento wood, is the signature dish, along with ackee and saltfish, patties, festival dumplings and rice and peas. Cricket and soccer are loved, but track and field is the pride of the nation; kids race barefoot at school sports days, and the national high school championships fill a stadium. Carnival and the Independence Day celebrations in August bring parades and dancing.
history:
The Taíno people lived on the island they called Xaymaca, "land of wood and water," when Columbus arrived in 1494. Spain ruled until 1655, when England seized the island and turned it into one of the world's biggest sugar producers, worked by hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans. Port Royal became a pirate haven until an earthquake sank much of it in 1692. Escaped slaves known as Maroons built free communities in the mountains and fought the British to a treaty in 1739.

A rebellion led by Sam Sharpe in 1831 helped push Britain to abolish slavery in 1834. Hard times followed for the freed people, and protests in the 1930s led to trade unions and political parties. Jamaica became independent on August 6, 1962. Since then its music and athletes have carried its culture around the world.
funFacts: Jamaica has won dozens of Olympic sprint medals, and Usain Bolt still holds the 100-meter and 200-meter world records.
Ian Fleming wrote all of his James Bond novels at his house, Goldeneye, on Jamaica's north coast.
Ackee, half of the national dish, is poisonous until it ripens and splits open naturally on the tree.
Jamaica's bobsled team competed at the 1988 Winter Olympics, inspiring the film Cool Runnings.
The doctor bird hummingbird lives only on Jamaica and has tail feathers longer than its body.
Jamaica built the first railway in the Caribbean in 1845, only two decades after the world's first passenger line.
